accepted.reason: Observation-target alignment is good: hospitalization rate plausibly lags an infection proxy, and delayed_I is explicitly recommended by the surveillance semantics. SEIRS is parsimonious for a single-season (n_train=31) series and avoids adding a potentially weakly identifiable H compartment. A 1-week fixed delay is a reasonable minimal choice given short admission/reporting lags and avoids extra states/parameters.

Kept as a delay ablation within the same structure; still uses delayed_I but with delay=0. While less aligned with hospitalization semantics, it is not structurally more complex and helps assess whether the series behaves near-contemporaneously in some windows. Identifiability risk remains low because no new compartments are introduced.

Kept as a neighboring delay ablation (delay=2) to probe plausible admission lag variation without changing mechanistic structure. Still aligns with hospitalization semantics and avoids explicit H. Risk is mainly phase misalignment rather than identifiability/over-complexity.

Minimal baseline (obs=I) is structurally simple and identifiable, but observation-target alignment is weaker for hospitalization-rate data where a lag is expected. Acceptable only as a sanity-check comparator; likely to incur systematic timing mismatch in short single-season data.

suggested_edits.edit: Clarify that delay is fixed and integer-week; note that if reporting/admission lag is nonstationary, this template may show phase error (already stated), but keep the structure unchanged.

Explicitly frame delay=2 as a robustness/uncertainty check rather than a primary mechanistic claim, since longer fixed delays can mimic smoothing and may confound with SEIRS time constants in short series.
Position as a strict baseline for observation mapping only; emphasize that it is intentionally misaligned with hospitalization semantics (no lag) and should not be over-interpreted mechanistically.
